design_detail: Steady-state pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic study over one 24-hour dosing interval in 18 people on stable once-daily methadone in the South Australian public methadone maintenance programme: 9 who reported no withdrawal between doses ('holders') and 9 who reported regular withdrawal before the next dose ('nonholders'), admitted to the programme's inpatient unit. Plasma racemic methadone was measured 13 times and withdrawal and opioid effects 11 times; 10 drug-free controls had the same effect measures without methadone or blood samples. Holders and nonholders compared with t tests; sigmoid Emax concentration-effect models. Read as the published PDF, Clin Pharmacol Ther 1999;65:685-694.
can_establish: Whether, in these 18 people on stable methadone, withdrawal symptoms rose and fell with plasma methadone over one dosing interval, and whether those who reported withdrawal before the next dose differed from those who did not in their level just before the dose, their overall exposure (AUC) or how fast their levels fell after the peak.
cannot_establish: That a faster fall in methadone levels causes withdrawal between doses (one interval, 9 per group, groups formed by self-report, the key difference significant only after excluding 2 people); how common such withdrawal is (the one-third figure comes from the authors' earlier survey, not this sample); or whether any change in treatment helps (none was tested).

sample.recruitment: Volunteers enrolled in the South Australian Public Methadone Maintenance Program for at least 6 months (range 6 months to 10 years) with no dose change for at least 2 months; 10 volunteer controls (p. 686).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded: pregnancy and positive HIV serology. How holder or nonholder status was established is not described beyond self-report (p. 686).
sample.demographics: 11 men and 7 women, aged 21-45 years, 60-94 kg. Holders and nonholders: age 36.3 and 34.3 years, time in the programme 2.3 and 3.9 years, weight 71.7 and 76.7 kg, men 67% and 56%, none significantly different (p. 690). Controls' ages and weights within the patients' range (p. 686).
sample.attrition: None reported. Concentration-effect models could be fitted for withdrawal in 9 of 18 people, for the MBG score in 10, pupil diameter in 12, pain threshold in 4 and respiratory rate in none (p. 690).
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected volunteers grouped by their own report, from one programme, long in treatment and stable; people with HIV excluded. The earlier survey the authors cite (34% of 114 patients were nonholders, p. 686) is not this sample.

exposure.measurement: Supervised dosing in the unit; plasma racemic methadone by HPLC (quantification limit 30 ng/mL; inter- and intra-assay inaccuracy under 8%) before the dose and 12 times over 23 hours; AUC by the linear trapezoidal method, peak and trough by inspection, and the maximum hourly rate of decline from peak to trough for each person (pp. 686-687).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: oral methadone syrup once daily at each person's usual stable dose, 0.12-1.9 mg/kg (7.5-130 mg) (p. 686); doses by group are not reported. In treatment at least 6 months, dose unchanged at least 2 months.
exposure.polysubstance: Most smoked cigarettes; urine positive for cannabinoids in 10, opioids other than methadone in 2, amphetamines in 2 and barbiturates in 1; 4 drank alcohol regularly, under 40 g a day; drug-positive urine did not differ between holders and nonholders (p. 686). The 2 with other opioids were holders and were excluded post hoc from one comparison (p. 690). Controls had used no psychoactive drug other than nicotine or caffeine for 2 months.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: people were tested on their usual methadone; other drug use was checked only by urinalysis.

comparison.controls: Main comparison: holders against nonholders. The 10 drug-free controls served only as a reference for the effect measures; they received no methadone and gave no blood (p. 686).
comparison.matching: Controls within the patients' ranges of age and weight; holders and nonholders not matched.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Methadone dose by group, years of opioid use before treatment, metabolic or genetic differences, other medicines, mood and anxiety, and expectations (people knew their own label).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Drug-free apart from nicotine and caffeine.

outcomes.instruments: Methadone Symptoms Checklist (the authors' 1997 instrument), withdrawal score 0-16; Morphine-Benzedrine Group scale of the Addiction Research Center Inventory (16 yes/no items) for positive opioid effects; pupil diameter from video under constant light; respiratory and pulse rate by observation; pain threshold to an electrical stimulus to the ear lobe (p. 687).
outcomes.validity_norms: The MBG scale is described as valid and reliable; no validity data are given for the withdrawal checklist.
outcomes.operationalization: Withdrawal severity is the number of withdrawal symptoms reported. A nonholder is a person who reports regular withdrawal during the dosing interval. The pharmacokinetic predictor is the maximum hourly fall in plasma methadone from peak to trough.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Five effect measures at up to 11 times by two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, at least five pharmacokinetic comparisons by t test, correlations and four sets of model parameters.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; the subjective measures were self-reported by people who knew which group they were in.

analysis.effect_sizes: Holders against nonholders (means, labelled as SD): plasma methadone before the dose 249 against 257 ng/mL (P > .05; range 44-614); peak-to-trough ratio 1.9 ± 0.1 against 1.7 ± 0.1 (P > .05); AUC 7.4 ± 5.0 against 8.2 ± 3.9 mg·h/L (P > .05). Maximum rate of decline 47.6 ± 21.3 against 74.5 ± 40.4 ng/mL/h, t = 1.77, P = .09; without 2 holders with other opioids in urine, 42.1 ± 20.8 against 74.5 ± 40.4, t = 2.10, stated P < .05 (two-sided P about .054 on 14 degrees of freedom, editors' calculation). Maximum rate of decline against withdrawal symptoms from peak to trough: r = 0.60 in all 18 (P < .01 in the text, P < .001 in the legend; about .009 by editors' calculation), r = 0.67 without the 2 (stated P < .001; about .005). Slope factors N: withdrawal 5.4 ± 0.9, MBG 5.1 ± 1.05, pupil 1.2 ± 0.1, pain threshold 2.8 ± 0.7, with no holder-nonholder differences (Table I).
analysis.preregistration_detail: None reported; ethics approval from the Royal Adelaide Hospital Research Ethics Committee (p. 686).
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract reports the subset comparison (74.5 against 42.1 ng/mL/h) as the group difference, without saying that two people were left out or that the full comparison was not significant (P = .09) (p. 685).
analysis.power: Not reported; 9 per group, and the concentration-effect comparisons rest on 4 to 7 people per group (Table I).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 18 people on stable methadone, withdrawal symptoms went down as plasma methadone rose and came back as it fell, with very steep concentration-effect curves for withdrawal and positive effects. Those reporting withdrawal before the next dose had the same level just before the dose and the same AUC as those who did not; their levels fell faster after the peak, a difference significant only after a post hoc exclusion of two people, with a two-sided P just above .05 by the editors' calculation.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that clinically important withdrawal is 'a consequence of more rapid decline in methadone concentration' (p. 685), and the Discussion that the differences 'are a consequence of pharmacokinetic rather than pharmacodynamic differences' (p. 692): causal conclusions from one dosing interval in 18 people, with the pharmacodynamic comparison resting on 4 to 7 people per group and the key difference on a subset. The Discussion also extends the 34% from the authors' earlier survey to other clinics and draws recommendations about dose scheduling and alternative medicines that this study did not test, while warning that data on the racemic mixture call for great caution about the mechanism (p. 692).

timeline.event: Nilsson et al.: smaller distribution volume and shorter half-life in people on methadone maintenance judged therapeutic failures (as described on p. 686; not read).
Hiltunen et al.: plasma methadone correlated with subjective withdrawal, less with objective measures (as described on p. 691; not read).

Dyer and White, the same group: 34% of 114 patients in the same programme reported regular withdrawal between doses, with no difference in demographics, other drug use or time in treatment (as described on p. 686; not read).
This study: first concurrent measurement of plasma methadone and withdrawal across a dosing interval in holders and nonholders.

replication.where_it_stands: Earlier studies cited by the authors point the same way (withdrawal follows falling methadone levels; people with poor responses clear or redistribute methadone differently), but no later replication of the holder-nonholder difference in the rate of decline was read for this card, and the enantiomer analysis the authors announced was not read.

funding.funder: Royal Adelaide Hospital Research Committee; scholarships to two authors (a Dawes Scholarship from the Royal Adelaide Hospital and a Dora Lush Postgraduate Scholarship from the NHMRC; a National Drug Strategy Postgraduate Research Scholarship) (p. 685).
funding.affiliations_note: University of Adelaide (clinical and experimental pharmacology; psychology) and the Royal Adelaide Hospital.

what_would_settle_it: A larger study of people on methadone, with withdrawal between doses measured on a standard scale rather than by self-label, the analysis planned in advance, R-methadone (the active enantiomer) measured, and doses reported by group; then randomized comparisons of treatment options for people who report such withdrawal.

domains.note: No adjustment; methadone dose by group not reported; other drug use present (two with other opioids); groups similar only on age, weight, sex and time in treatment.
Plasma methadone by a validated HPLC assay at 13 times during supervised steady-state dosing.
Volunteers chosen by self-reported holder status; two holders excluded post hoc from the key comparison.
Usual dose, supervised, during one inpatient day.
Concentration-effect models fitted in only 9 of 18 for withdrawal and 4 for pain; people without a fit were dropped from those analyses.
Withdrawal self-reported on the authors' checklist by people who knew their label; no blinding reported.
The key difference is significant only in a post hoc subset that the abstract presents as the result; several P values do not match their test statistics.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A small, carefully measured pharmacokinetic study whose main group comparison is fragile: the two groups were formed by self-report, the rate-of-decline difference was not significant in the full sample (P = .09) and borderline after excluding two people, and the abstract reports only the subset. The within-person link between falling levels and withdrawal (r = 0.60 across all 18) is the sturdier finding. The study can be cited for that link and for the absence of a difference in levels just before the dose; it cannot be cited as showing that a faster fall causes withdrawal, or for any treatment change.

verification.first_pass_by: AI (Claude, reading agent), AI reader 122 (first reader)
verification.source_read: PDF pp. 685-694 (PDFs/Methadone-Buprenorphine/Dyer_1999_InterdoseWithdrawalPKPD.pdf), the published article read in full, including Table I (checked on a 110 dpi rendering of p. 691), the legends of Figures 1-3 (the plotted values were not extracted), acknowledgements, funding note and reference list; extracted once with pdftotext.

key_findings.finding: Sample: 9 self-reported holders and 9 nonholders on once-daily methadone, in treatment 6 months to 10 years, dose unchanged at least 2 months; 11 men and 7 women, aged 21-45; most smoked; urine positive for cannabinoids in 10, other opioids in 2, amphetamines in 2, barbiturates in 1; 10 drug-free controls.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Patients and control subjects, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Over the dosing interval, withdrawal symptoms were significantly more frequent in the 18 patients than in controls at all times and least severe from 2 to about 8 hours after the dose; the MBG positive-effect score peaked 2-3 hours after the dose and returned to baseline by 7 hours; pain threshold was raised for about 6 hours; pupils were smaller than in controls throughout; respiratory rate fell 3 hours after the dose and was faster than in controls before the dose and from about 9 hours after it.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacodynamic responses: Subjective responses and Objective responses paragraphs; Figure 1 legend (p. 688)

key_findings.finding: Withdrawal was significantly higher in nonholders and strongly inversely related to plasma methadone in both groups. Plasma methadone before the dose: 249 ng/mL in holders and 257 ng/mL in nonholders (P > .05; range 44-614); 6 of 9 in each group were above 200 ng/mL. Peaks at about 3 hours, not different, range 69-980 ng/mL. Peak-to-trough ratio 1.9 ± 0.1 and 1.7 ± 0.1 (P > .05). AUC 7.4 ± 5.0 and 8.2 ± 3.9 mg·h/L (P > .05). AUC correlated with weight-adjusted dose (r = 0.74, P < .001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacokinetics and withdrawal severity in holders and nonholders, 1st paragraph; Figure 2

key_findings.finding: Maximum rate of decline in plasma methadone: holders 47.6 ± 21.3 and nonholders 74.5 ± 40.4 ng/mL/h (t = 1.77, P = .09); without the two people with other opioids in urine, 42.1 ± 20.8 against 74.5 ± 40.4 (t = 2.10, stated P < .05). Correlation between maximum rate of decline and mean number of withdrawal symptoms from peak to trough in all 18: r = 0.60 (P < .01); without the two, r = 0.67 (P < .001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacokinetics and withdrawal severity, 2nd paragraph; Figure 3 and legend
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: t = 2.10 on 14 degrees of freedom gives two-sided P of about .054; r = 0.67 with 16 people gives P of about .005. The two excluded people were holders (the nonholder values are unchanged).

key_findings.finding: Slope factors N (Table I): withdrawal 5.4 ± 0.9 (holders 6.1, n = 4; nonholders 4.9, n = 5), MBG 5.1 ± 1.05 (n = 10), pupil diameter 1.2 ± 0.1 (n = 12), pain threshold 2.8 ± 0.7 (n = 4); EC50 for withdrawal 301.8 ± 292.1 ng/mL; no holder-nonholder differences (P > .05). N differed between withdrawal and pupil diameter (P < .0001), MBG and pupil (P < .006), pain and pupil (P < .007), but not withdrawal and pain (P < .054).
key_findings.locator: Results › Plasma concentration-effect relationships, 1st paragraph (p. 690); Table I (p. 691)

key_findings.finding: Background from the authors' earlier survey in the same programme: 34% of a non-selected sample of 114 patients regularly experienced withdrawal between doses, with average daily doses above 60 mg and no differences in demographics, other drug use or time in the programme; plasma levels were not measured there.
key_findings.note: Second-hand within this paper (Dyer and White, 1997, not read).

key_findings.finding: The authors draw recommendations about dose scheduling and alternative medicines (buprenorphine, LAAM, slow-release morphine, a slow-release methadone) and caution that analyses of racemic methadone call for great caution about the mechanism; none of the recommendations was tested in this study.
key_findings.note: The scheduling recommendation is not reproduced here (no regimens on the site).

reporting_issues.issue: The subset comparison of the maximum rate of decline (42.1 ± 20.8 for 7 holders against 74.5 ± 40.4 for 9 nonholders, t = 2.10) is reported as P < .05; on 14 degrees of freedom the two-sided P is about .054 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The only reported pharmacokinetic difference between the groups is borderline even after a post hoc exclusion; it is not significant in the full sample (P = .09).

reporting_issues.issue: For r = 0.60 in 18 patients the text gives P < .01 and the Figure 3 legend P < .001 (about .009 by editors' calculation); for r = 0.67 in 16 the text gives P < .001 (about .005).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the correlations hold at P < .01.

reporting_issues.issue: Values are labelled mean ± SD (p. 689; Table I), but the peak-to-trough ratios 1.9 ± 0.1 and 1.7 ± 0.1 with P > .05 fit standard errors (with SDs of 0.1 and 9 per group, P would be below .001), and the all-patient slope factors for MBG and pupil diameter equal the standard errors of the pooled subgroup values (editors' calculation); the withdrawal row (5.4 ± 0.9) fits neither.
reporting_issues.consequence: Variability between people is larger than the table suggests; the ± values cannot be read as SDs without checking.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the maximal rate of decline as 74.5 against 42.1 ng/mL/h (p. 685), the subset values, without saying that two people were excluded or that the full-sample comparison (47.6 against 74.5) was not significant.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader of the abstract alone would overrate the group difference.

reporting_issues.issue: Methadone doses are given only as a range for all 18 (7.5-130 mg; p. 686), not by group.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether holders and nonholders differed in dose cannot be checked; similar AUCs (p. 690) only partly address this.
